deep_dive_html:
The Peril of All-Inclusive Personal Guarantees

For salon owners, the personal guarantee is often the most dangerous instrument in a commercial lease. While many tenants accept a guarantee to ensure lease execution, the true danger lies in the scope of the obligation. Landlords frequently draft guarantees that encompass not just the base rent, but the entirety of 'Additional Rent.' This includes Common Area Maintenance (CAM), real estate taxes, insurance, and even the landlord's legal fees incurred during a default.

In the salon industry, where margins are tightly controlled by labor and supply costs, an unexpected spike in CAM—driven by landlord mismanagement or unexpected building repairs—can render a location unprofitable. If your personal guarantee is uncapped and includes these variable costs, you are not just guaranteeing your rent; you are personally underwriting the landlord's operational inefficiencies and the building's capital expenditures. This creates a direct pipeline from a business downturn to the seizure of your personal assets, including your home and savings. Furthermore, many landlords attempt to include 'consequential damages' or 'attorney fees' within the guarantee, meaning a simple dispute over a repair could trigger a personal debt that far exceeds the value of the leasehold.

Implementing Market-Standard Protections

To mitigate this risk, a sophisticated tenant must negotiate a 'Base Rent Only' guarantee. This structure ensures that your personal liability is strictly limited to the fixed monthly rent, effectively insulating your personal estate from the volatility of operating expenses. If the landlord refuses to strip out additional rent, the next best defense is a 'Burn-off' provision or a 'Good Guy' clause.

  • Base Rent Limitation: Restricts the guarantee to the fixed monthly rent amount, excluding all CAM, taxes, and insurance.
  • Guaranty Burn-off: A clause stating that the personal guarantee expires after a set period, such as 24 or 36 months, of continuous, timely payments.
  • Good Guy Clause: Limits your personal liability to the period during which you occupy the premises and provide proper notice of surrender, preventing liability from accruing after you vacate.
